summary: Describes an experimental Nonce Destination Option used only with ILNP for IPv6 (ILNPv6). It is part of the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol, an experimental, evolutionary enhancement to IP, and comes from the IRTF Routing Research Group.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6744 defines an IPv6 option that carries a random number shared by the two ends of an ILNP session. A machine off the path cannot guess that number, so it cannot forge packets that look like part of the session. The option also marks the session as an ILNP session, so the two ends know how to talk.

subtitle: A random value in every IPv6 packet of an ILNP session, so an outside machine cannot guess its way in.

tldr.problem: An ILNP session identifies its endpoints by a stable identifier, so a machine that is not on the path can try to inject packets and take the session over.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines an IPv6 Destination Options option that carries an unpredictable random value, the nonce, known only to the two endpoints. Its presence in the first packets of a session also tells the other side that ILNP is in use for that session.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document from the IRTF Routing Research Group. The option protects only against off-path attacks, and the memo says plainly that it is not a substitute for IPsec.

today: RFC 6744 is an Experimental document from November 2012, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is one of a set of ILNP documents from the IRTF Routing Research Group, and it defines only the nonce option for ILNPv6; the ILNP architecture itself is described in a separate document.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
The Identifier-Locator Network Protocol is an experimental, evolutionary enhancement to IP, and ILNP has multiple instantiations. This memo describes an experimental Nonce Destination Option used only with ILNP for IPv6, and it is a product of the IRTF Routing Research Group.

The memo is part of the ILNP document set. It notes that the ideas it contains have had much broader review than the Routing Research Group itself, and that the views were considered controversial by the group, which nevertheless reached a consensus that the document should be published.

The option is carried in the IPv6 Destination Options header and is used only in ILNPv6 sessions, never with classic IPv6 sessions. It provides two functions. First, it provides protection against off-path attacks for packets when ILNPv6 is in use. Second, it provides a signal during initial network-layer session creation that ILNPv6 is proposed for use with that session rather than classic IPv6. The memo says this second function is particularly important for ensuring that ILNP is both incrementally deployable and backwards compatible with IPv6, and consequently the option must not be used except by an ILNPv6-capable node.

Each nonce value is unidirectional. Since packets often travel asymmetric paths between two correspondents, having separate nonces for each direction limits the number of on-path nodes that can easily learn a session's nonce. A typical TCP session therefore has two different nonce values in use, one from the local node to the correspondent node and a different one from the correspondent node back.
sections.plainLanguage: The option does two jobs. It proves that a packet really belongs to the session, because only the two ends know the random number. And it tells the other side, in the very first packets, that this session is an ILNP session and not an ordinary IPv6 one.

sections.title: Syntax of the Nonce Option
sections.content:
The Nonce Option is carried within an IPv6 Destination Options header. More than one option might be inside that header, but at most one Nonce Option exists in a given IPv6 packet. A system that receives a packet containing more than one Nonce Option should discard the packet as an authentication failure, rather than passing it up to a transport protocol or to ICMP, and should log the event with the source and destination locator and identifier, the upper-layer protocol if any, the transport-layer port numbers if any, as a security fault in accordance with local logging policies.

The memo notes that IPv6 Destination Options headers, and the options they carry, are extremely uncommon in the deployed Internet, so the Nonce Option would commonly be the only IPv6 Destination Option present in a given packet. If a Common Architecture Label IPv6 Security Option label is also present in the same header, that option should precede the Nonce Option, and the Nonce Option should precede other possible options in the same header.

The header holds a Next Header field, an 8-bit selector identifying the type of header immediately following the Destination Options header, using the same values as the IPv4 Protocol field, and an Hdr Ext Len field giving the length of the header in 8-octet units, not including the first 8 octets. The option itself has an Option Type field holding the value 0x8B, which is 139, and an Option Length field giving the length in octets of the Nonce Value field. That value must be selected so the enclosing Destination Options header complies with the IPv6 header alignment rules; common values are 4 when the nonce is 32 bits and 12 when it is 96 bits.

The Nonce Value is an unpredictable cryptographically random value used to prevent off-path attacks on an ILNP session. The field has variable length, with the length given by the Option Length field, and the overall Destination Options header must comply with the IPv6 header alignment rules. Implementations must support sending and receiving 32-bit and 96-bit nonce values.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is a small addition to an IPv6 extension header. Its length field says how long the random number is, and the header as a whole must line up on byte boundaries the way IPv6 requires.

sections.title: Transport Effects and Location Changes
sections.content:
When the initial packets of an IPv6 session contain the Nonce Destination Option, ILNPv6 is in use for that network-layer session. When a network-layer session is using ILNPv6, the transport-layer pseudo-header calculations must set to zero the high-order 64 bits, the Locator or Routing Prefix, of each IPv6 address. The effect is that the transport layer is no longer aware of the topological network location of either node in the session. The rule applies to unicast ILNPv6 sessions and also to multicast and anycast ILNPv6 sessions.

When a node has a change in its Locator set that causes all previously valid Locators to become invalid, the node must send an ICMP Locator Update message, containing the Nonce Option with the appropriate nonce value, to each of its correspondents.

In the deployed Internet, packets sometimes arrive at a destination out of order. A receiving node must drop a packet arriving from a correspondent if the source locator of the received packet is not in the receiving node's Identifier-Locator Communication Cache set of correspondent locators, unless that packet contains a Nonce Option with the appropriate nonce value for that source identifier and destination identifier pair. This is done to reduce the risk of ILNP session hijacking or interference attacks. The node that has had all its previously valid locators become invalid must therefore include the Nonce Option with the appropriate nonce value in all packets, data or otherwise, to all correspondents for at least three round-trip times for each correspondent. The memo notes that an implementation need not actually calculate round-trip time values and could use a fixed timer long enough to cover the longest round-trip path, such as one minute. This gratuitous authentication ensures the correspondent can authenticate any received packet, even if the Locator Update control message arrives and is processed after some other packet using the new locators. If an ILNP session is using IPsec, IPsec should continue to be used even if one or more participating nodes change location, because IP Security for ILNP binds only to the identifiers and not to the locators, so a change of locator value has no impact on it. Since mobility and multihoming are functionally equivalent for ILNP, the same rules apply to either.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rules follow. The transport layer stops caring where the nodes are, since only the identifiers matter. And when a node moves, it stamps the nonce into everything it sends for a short while, so the other side can tell the new packets apart from old ones that arrive out of order.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility and Incremental Deployment
sections.content:
This option must not be present in an IPv6 packet unless the packet is part of an ILNPv6 session. The presence or absence of the option in the initial packets of a new IPv6 session is an important indication of whether the session is using classic IPv6 or ILNPv6. ILNPv6 nodes must include the option in the first few packets of each ILNPv6 session, must include it in all ICMP messages generated by endpoints participating in an ILNPv6 session, and may include it in any and all packets of an ILNPv6 session. It is recommended that the option be included in all packets of the session if the packet loss for that session is known to be much higher than normal.

If a node supports ILNP and wants to be able to receive incoming new ILNP sessions, then its fully qualified domain name should have one or more Node Identifier records and one or more Locator records associated with it in the DNS. When a host initiates a new IP session it normally performs a DNS lookup to determine the address of the responder, and a host enhanced to support the Identifier/Locator Split operating mode should look for Node Identifier and Locator records in any received DNS replies. DNS servers that support Identifier and Locator records might include them as additional data in all replies to queries for A or AAAA records.

If the initiator supports ILNP and learns from the DNS data that the responder also supports ILNP, then the initiator should attempt to use ILNP for new sessions with that responder. It must generate an unpredictable, cryptographically random ILNP nonce value, must store it in the local Identifier-Locator Communication Cache, and must include the ILNP Nonce Destination Option in its initial packets. If the responder supports ILNP and receives initial packets containing the option, it thereby learns that the initiator supports ILNP and uses ILNPv6 for the new session. If the responder supports ILNP and receives initial packets without the option, it learns that the initiator does not support ILNP and uses classic IPv6 for the session.

If the responder does not support ILNP and receives initial packets containing the option, it must drop the packet and send an ICMP Parameter Problem error message back to the initiator. The memo observes that this is not expected to need to be coded into non-ILNP nodes, since it is the normal behaviour for nodes receiving unknown option headers. If the initiator either does not receive a response in a timely manner and does not receive an ICMP Unreachable error message, or receives an ICMP Parameter Problem error message, it infers that the responder cannot support ILNP, and should try again to create the session using classic IPv6, without the option.
sections.plainLanguage: The option doubles as a signal. If it is in the opening packets, both sides use ILNP for that session; if it is not, they fall back to ordinary IPv6. A node that does not know the option drops the packet and complains, and the sender then retries without it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Nonce Destination Option is used only for ILNPv6 sessions, because it is part of the backwards compatibility and incremental deployment approach for ILNP. It must not be used with classic IPv6 sessions.

The option seeks only to provide protection against off-path attacks on an IP session. Ordinary IPv6 is vulnerable to on-path attacks unless IPsec is in use. The memo is explicit that the option exists to provide non-cryptographic protection for ILNP sessions, protection equivalent to that of IP sessions that do not use IPsec.

When ILNPv6 is in use, the option must be included in any ICMP control messages, such as ICMP Unreachable and ICMP Locator Update messages, sent by participants in the session, even if IPsec is also in use. Certain ICMP messages, for example a Packet Too Big message, might be generated by transit devices that are not aware of the nonce in use, so they cannot include it; the memo notes that this is also true of classic IPv6 in the same operational situations, so it does not create a new security issue.

For ILNPv6 sessions, ICMP control messages received from a participant that lack a Nonce Destination Option must be discarded as forgeries, and the security event should be logged with details of the received packet. Messages that have a Nonce Destination Option but do not have the correct nonce value must also be discarded as forgeries and logged. Longer nonce values provide greater resistance to random guessing, so ILNPv6 sessions operating in higher risk environments should also use the cryptographic authentication provided by IP Security for ILNP, and using IPsec does not remove the need for the nonce option.

As a performance optimisation, when both the Nonce Option and IPsec are present in a packet and the nonce has not been encrypted, the nonce value could be checked for validity before beginning IPsec processing, so that an off-path attacker cannot force the recipient to perform expensive cryptographic computations on received control packets. In environments with data at differing sensitivity levels, it is recommended that the nonce option be encrypted using ESP transport mode or tunnel mode, to reduce the covert channel bandwidth potential created by the option and to prevent a node at one sensitivity level from attacking a session at a different level. Multi-Level Secure systems should use different nonce values for sessions with different sensitivity levels, and should store the sensitivity label information for each session in the implementation's Identifier-Locator Communication Cache.

As the option sits in the IPv6 Destination Options header rather than the Hop-by-Hop Option Header, its presence ought not disturb routers along the path. Many deployed modern IP routers, for both IPv4 and IPv6, have been explicitly configured to ignore all IP Options, even the Router Alert option, when forwarding packets not addressed to the router itself, to preclude the use of IP options as a denial-of-service attack vector.
sections.plainLanguage: The nonce stops an outsider guessing its way into a session. It does nothing against a machine on the path, and the memo says so: for that you need IPsec. Long random values and IPsec together are what a careful deployment should use.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Consistent with the procedures of RFC 2780, IANA has assigned a new IPv6 Destination Option Type value of 0x8B.

The Nonce Option must not change in transit and must be included in IP Authentication Header calculations. If an end system receives an IPv6 packet containing this option but does not recognise the option, it must discard the packet and, regardless of whether the received packet's destination address was a multicast address, send an ICMPv6 Parameter Problem, Code 2, Unrecognised IPv6 Option Encountered, message to the received packet's source IPv6 address, pointing to the unrecognised option type.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA assigned the option type number. The option must not be altered by routers, it counts towards the packet's authentication checksum, and a node that does not recognise it must drop the packet and report it.

viz.caption: WHAT THE NONCE DOES AND DOES NOT PROTECT

items.title: Off-path attacks
items.text: A random value only the two endpoints know stops a machine elsewhere guessing its way into the session.

items.title: On-path attacks
items.text: The option does not help against a machine on the path; that requires IPsec.

items.title: ICMP messages
items.text: Control messages in an ILNPv6 session must carry the nonce, and one without it or with the wrong value is discarded as a forgery.

items.title: Longer nonces
items.text: Longer values resist random guessing better, so higher risk environments should use them and IPsec as well.

items.title: One nonce per direction
items.text: Each direction has its own nonce, so fewer machines on the path learn it.
